paragraphs.heading: Fish with bony skeletons
paragraphs.text: Bony fish, known to scientists as Osteichthyes, are vertebrates whose inner skeleton is made mainly of bone. The name comes from the Greek words for bone and fish. They stand in contrast to cartilaginous fish, and to some extinct groups, whose skeletons are mostly cartilage. Most fish alive today are bony fish, spread across 45 orders, more than 435 families and 28,000 species.

paragraphs.heading: Two great branches
paragraphs.text: The group splits into ray-finned fish, which include most living fish, and lobe-finned fish, which gave rise to every land vertebrate. The oldest bony fish fossils date back roughly 436 million years, to the early Silurian. Their teeth are arranged in a pattern partway between sharks and true bony fish. Oddly, these early members had skeletons still mostly made of cartilage. What set them apart was a set of pouches off the front of the gut that later became swim bladders and lungs.

paragraphs.heading: From air pouch to lung
paragraphs.text: In early bony fish, a simple pouch on each side of the gullet let them gulp air when the water held little oxygen. In ray-finned fish these pouches became swim bladders, whose changing size adjusts how buoyant the fish is. In the lobe-finned line that led to land animals, they became the lungs of amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. Lungfish and some others can still breathe with lungs or with a swim bladder rich in blood vessels. Other bony fish take in oxygen through the skin, the intestines or the stomach.

paragraphs.heading: Fins and gill covers
paragraphs.text: Early bony fish had fleshy, paddle-like fins rather than the fin spines most modern fish have. Lobe-finned fish grew jointed bones inside their paired fins, and these became the limbs of four-legged animals. Bony fish also gained a pair of gill covers, the opercula, which pump water over the gills. That lets them breathe while staying still instead of having to keep swimming.

paragraphs.heading: Scales under the skin
paragraphs.text: Unlike cartilaginous fish, bony fish lack placoid scales; their scales sit beneath the outer skin and do not pierce it. There are three kinds: cosmoid, ganoid and teleost scales, and teleost scales come in two forms, cycloid and ctenoid. All of them grow from a base of bone. Teleost scales have just one bone layer, while ganoid scales stack two layers of bone under a coat of enamel. Cosmoid scales have the same two layers plus dentin between the enamel and the bone.

paragraphs.heading: Where tetrapods belong
paragraphs.text: Bony fish used to be ranked as a class, recognised by a swim bladder, three pairs of gill arches under a bony cover and a mostly bony skeleton. Defined that way the class was paraphyletic, because the shared ancestor of all bony fish also has land vertebrates among its descendants. Since 2013, widely cited studies have drawn family trees that count land vertebrates as bony fish. On that view Osteichthyes means the same as another name, Euteleostomi.

paragraphs.heading: Ways of life
paragraphs.text: Bony fish were cold-blooded from the start, with body temperature set by the water. Yet some big ocean species, such as the opah, swordfish and tuna, have each evolved some ability to keep themselves warm. Their diets cover every option: plant eaters, meat eaters, filter feeders, detritus feeders and even blood feeders. Some species are hermaphrodites, and in most the eggs are fertilised outside the body.
